notes.short: Two lines, two ways: the righteous and the wicked
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. Both lines speak of a way: the LORD guards one, and the other perishes.

lines.words: For the LORD guards the path of the righteous,
but the way of the wicked will perish.

original.note: In Hebrew both lines use the same word, derekh, “way”; the BSB says “path”, then “way”.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) sets the way of the ungodly against the way of the righteous. Barnes calls verses 4 to 6 a strong contrast between the unrighteous and the righteous. Henry: the Lord approves the way of the righteous and is angry at the way of the wicked, which shall perish.

cites.quote: God knows this way, which on this very account also unfailingly reaches its goal. On the contrary, the way of the ungodly … perishes, because left to itself
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The condition of the unrighteous, or the strong contrast between the unrighteous and the righteous
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Lord approves and is well pleased with the way of the righteous, and therefore, under the influence of his gracious smiles, it shall prosper and end well; but he is angry at the way of the wicked, all they do is offensive to him, and therefore it shall perish, and they in it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The godly man is “like a tree planted”
notes.about: The man who delights in the LORD's law is said to be like a tree planted by streams of water. It is set in place and watered, not left to grow wild, so it bears fruit in season and its leaf stays green. Verse 4 gives the opposite picture: chaff.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: like a tree planted by streams of water
figure.means: the man who meditates on God's word: rooted, fed by it, fruitful and lasting

original.note: In Hebrew “streams” is peleg, from a root meaning to divide: channels or brooks that carry water.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Simile: the man who meditates in God's word is planted and protected like a tree in a garden. Henry calls it a similitude, the rivers being the means of grace; Barnes, a beautiful image of a tree set out with care where its roots have water; Delitzsch says God's word is to that man what the brook is to the tree.

cites.quote: Here, the similitude tells us that the man who meditates in God’s word is planted and protected, just as a tree in a garden is cared for as a “tree of the field” is not.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: His blessedness is here illustrated by a similitude ... He shall be like a tree, fruitful and flourishing. ... That he is placed by the means of grace, here called the rivers of water
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This is presented in the form of a very beautiful image - a tree planted where its roots would have abundance of water. ... It is not a tree that springs up spontaneously, but one that is set out in a favorable place, and that is cultivated with care. ... properly means divisions; and then, channels, canals, trenches, branching-cuts, brooks.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: What a richly flowing brook is to the tree that is planted on its bank, such is the word of God to him who devotes himself to it
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The wicked are “like chaff driven off by the wind”
notes.about: The wicked are likened to chaff, the light husk the wind blows away when grain is winnowed. Set against the planted tree of verse 3, the picture shows them without root or fruit, of no worth, and soon swept away.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: like chaff driven off by the wind
figure.means: the wicked: without root or fruit, worthless, and soon gone

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Simile and calls the contrast between the driven chaff and the planted tree most striking and solemn. Barnes says the winnowed chaff pictures the worthlessness of the wicked; Delitzsch: without root below or fruit above, worthless and unstable; Henry: of no worth in God's account, with no solidity.

cites.quote: The contrast between the driven chaff and the “planted” tree is most striking and solemn. The two comparisons are the great features of the Psalm
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This very naturally and appropriately furnished an illustration of the destiny of the wicked. Compared with the righteous, they were like the worthless chaff driven away by the wind. ... The idea thus suggested, therefore, is that of intrinsic worthlessness.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: are the opposite of a tree planted by the water-courses ... without root below, without fruit above, devoid of all the vigour and freshness of life ... thus utterly worthless and unstable.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: whereas the righteous are like valuable, useful, fruitful trees, they are like the chaff which the wind drives away ... They are like chaff, of no worth at all in God's account, how highly soever they may value themselves. ... They are light and vain; they have no substance in them, no solidity
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The Lord “laughs”: His scorn told in human terms
notes.about: The One enthroned in heaven laughs at the rulers who plot against the LORD and His Anointed. Laughter is spoken of God in human terms, to show His contempt for their vain plans. It can also show His calm as He carries out His own. Psalm 37:13 speaks of His laughter in the same way.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God's contempt for the rulers' vain plotting against Him and His Anointed

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia, among the human actions spoken of God, as laughing. Clarke calls the words spoken after the manner of men, for utter contempt of their efforts; Barnes says the same, and that God goes calmly on with His purposes and looks on their efforts with contempt; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a bold figure, the laughter of supreme contempt.

cites.quote: Laughing. ... “He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord ... shall have them in derision.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Shall laugh. Words spoken after the manner of men; shall utterly contemn their puny efforts; shall beat down their pride, assuage their malice, and confound their devices.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Will smile at their vain attempts; will not be disturbed or agitated by their efforts; will go calmly on in the execution of his purposes. ... This is, of course, to be regarded as spoken after the manner of men ... There is included also the idea that he will look with contempt on their vain and futile efforts.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: By a figure whose boldness is only allowable to an inspired writer, God's conduct and language in view of this opposition are now related. ... shall laugh--in supreme contempt; their vain rage excites His derision.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: God's “fingers”: the heavens are His own handiwork
notes.about: David calls the heavens the work of God's fingers, speaking of God as a craftsman working with his hands. The picture shows the heavens as God's own direct work; it can also speak of the skill and the ease with which He made them.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God's own direct act in making the heavens, which can also speak of the skill and ease of His work

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia: a finger is given to God for the putting forth of His power to form, His own direct act. Albert Barnes says fingers may point to skill rather than strength. Henry says God made the heavens easily, with no outstretched arm, and with fine care, as an artist works with his fingers.

cites.quote: A Finger is attributed to God, to denote the putting forth of His formative power, and the direct and immediate act of God.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The work of thy fingers - Which thy fingers have made. The fingers are the instruments by which we construct a piece of work - perhaps indicating skill rather than strength; and hence so used in respect to God, as it is by his skill that the heavens have been made.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: They are therefore his, because they are the work of his fingers. He made them; he made them easily. The stretching out of the heavens needed not any outstretched arm; it was done with a word; it was but the work of his fingers. He made them with very great curiosity and fineness, like a nice piece of work which the artist makes with his fingers.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The LORD pictured as a shepherd caring for his flock
notes.about: David calls the LORD his shepherd. The picture shows God’s care for His people: He feeds, leads and guards them as a shepherd does his flock, so they lack nothing they truly need. Jesus later says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.means: the LORD, who feeds, leads and guards His people as a shepherd does his sheep

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metaphor: the LORD is shown as a Shepherd who tends His people. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a metaphor from pastoral life for God’s care; Calvin, the similitude of a shepherd; Henry says David, once a shepherd, illustrates by it God’s care of His people; Barnes calls it a comparison that speaks of tender care and protection.
notes.limit: Some of the writers also see Christ in this Shepherd, pointing to John 10; the note claims only the picture of the LORD’s care.

cites.quote: Here, we have a Metaphor; and in it a great and blessed truth is set forth by the representation of Jehovah as a Shepherd. It is He who tends his People, and does more for them than any earthly shepherd does for his sheep
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Under a metaphor borrowed from scenes of pastoral life, with which David was familiar, he describes God's providential care in providing refreshment, guidance, protection, and abundance
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Under the similitude of a shepherd, he commends the care which God, in his providence, had exercised towards him. His language implies that God had no less care of him than a shepherd has of the sheep who are committed to his charge.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Time was when David was himself a shepherd; ... so he knew by experience the cares and tender affections of a good shepherd towards his flock. ... By this therefore he illustrates God's care of his people
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The comparison of the care which God extends over his people to that of a shepherd for his flock is one that would naturally occur to those who were accustomed to pastoral life. ... The idea which the language suggests is that of tender care; protection; particular attention to the young and the feeble
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: As a deer longs for water, so the soul for God
notes.about: The psalmist likens his longing for God to a thirsty deer that pants for streams of water. The picture shows how strong his desire is to come before God again, as the next verse asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?”

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You
figure.means: the soul’s strong longing for God, like a thirsty deer’s longing for water

original.note: In Hebrew the same verb, arag, is used of the deer and of the soul; the BSB says “pants”, then “longs”. The deer longs for water below it, the soul for God above.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among the similes built on as and so. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the poet compares his soul’s thirst for God to a stag’s, the hind’s longing going down, the soul’s up. Henry: he compares it to the panting of a hart. Barnes calls it an image of the earnest longing of a soul after God; Clarke likens the spent hart to the psalmist panting for God.
notes.limit: Some writers picture the deer as hunted and spent; the verse itself speaks only of its longing for water.

cites.quote: The hart panting, and the soul longing (Psa 42:1 (2)).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The poet compares the thirsting of his soul after God to the thirsting of a stag. ... על and אל point to the difference in the object of the longing, viz., the hind has this object beneath herself, the soul above itself
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He compares it to the panting of a hart, or deer, which is naturally hot and dry, especially of a hunted buck, after the water-brooks. Thus earnestly does a gracious soul desire communion with God
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Nothing could more beautifully or appropriately describe the earnest longing of a soul after God, in the circumstances of the psalmist, than this image.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The hart feels himself almost entirely spent; he is nearly hunted down; the dogs are in full pursuit; he is parched with thirst; and in a burning heat pants after the water ... Thus pursued, spent, and nearly ready to give up the ghost, the psalmist pants for God, for the living God!
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: David's tears kept in God's book
notes.about: David says his tears are already in God's book. A book is a human thing spoken of God: it tells that He has noted every tear and will not forget them. The bottle beside it pictures the same care.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God's sure remembrance of David's tears, spoken of as a record He keeps

original.note: In Hebrew the last words, in Your book (sifrah), take up the first verb, taken account of (safar), so the verse ends where it began.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists this verse under Anthropopatheia, where a book is attributed to God. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the verse figuratively sets forth that God gathers His saints' tears as in a bottle and notes them as in a memorial (Malachi 3:16); he ties the last words to the first verb. Henry and Barnes read the book as God's book of remembrance: the tears are recorded, not forgotten.

cites.quote: A Book is attributed to God. … A Book of Life
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: the closing clause הלא בּספרתך unites with ספרתּה in the first member of the verse. … The fact thus figuratively set forth, viz., that God collects the tears of His saints as it were in a bottle, and notes them together with the things which call them forth as in a memorial (Mal 3:16)
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: God has a bottle and a book for his people's tears, both those for their sins and those for their afflictions. … That he will remember them and review them, as we do the accounts we have booked.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In thy book of remembrance; are they not numbered and recorded so that they will not be forgotten?
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “Righteousness and peace have kissed” like friends
notes.about: The psalm speaks of loving devotion, faithfulness, righteousness and peace as if they were persons. Two meet together and two kiss, as friends do. The picture shows them joined in full harmony, with none at odds with another.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed
figure.means: these four, pictured as friends who meet and kiss, joined in full harmony

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a charming allegory: mercy meets fidelity like one guardian angel meeting another, and righteousness and peace kiss like two inseparable brothers. Barnes: they kiss as estranged friends do when made friends again, blending in harmony. Henry, among other readings, takes the kiss as the harmony of God's mercy and truth, righteousness and peace, in salvation.
notes.limit: The writers agree on the picture, not on where the meeting is found: in God's renewed blessing on His people and their land, or in the salvation Christ brings, where mercy and justice agree.

cites.quote: The possessions that make a people truly happy and prosperous are mentioned under a charming allegory ... Mercy or loving-kindness walks along the streets of Jerusalem, and there meets fidelity, like one guardian angel meeting the other. Righteousness and peace or prosperity, these two inseparable brothers, kiss each other there, and fall lovingly into each other's arms.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Have kissed each other - As friends and lovers do ... but they have been now united as separated and alienated friends are, and have embraced each other as such friends do; that is, they blend together in beautiful harmony.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Of the harmony of the divine attributes in the Messiah's undertaking. ... God's mercy and truth, and his righteousness and peace, have kissed each other; that is, the great affair of our salvation is so well contrived ... that God may have mercy upon poor sinners, and be at peace with them, without any wrong to his truth and righteousness.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Three lines that climb as the floods rise
notes.about: Each line goes a step further: the floods have risen, then raised their voice, then lift up their pounding waves. The first two lines tell what has happened, and the third what is happening still. The next verse answers that the LORD on high is above them all.

lines.words: The floodwaters have risen, O LORD;
the rivers have raised their voice;
the seas lift up their pounding waves.

original.note: In Hebrew all three lines use the same word, rivers, which the BSB gives as floodwaters, rivers and seas, and the same verb, lift up. The first two verbs tell what has happened; the third tells what goes on still.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the thought is unfolded across the lines, the first two verbs telling what has taken place and the third what is still taking place. Henry reads the floods lifting up their voice as terror, and then their waves as real danger, and verse 4 as the anchor in that storm: God is on high, above them.

cites.quote: These rivers … have lifted up, have lifted up their murmur, the rivers lift up their roaring. The thought is unfolded in a so-called "parallelism with reservation." The perfects affirm what has taken place, the future that which even now as yet is taking place.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A threatening storm supposed: The floods have lifted up, O Lord! (to God himself the remonstrance is made) the floods have lifted up their voice, which speaks terror; nay, they have lifted up their waves, which speaks real danger. … The Lord himself is mightier. Let this keep our minds fixed, (1.) That God is on high, above them
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Rivers clap their hands, mountains sing
notes.about: The psalm calls the rivers to clap their hands and the mountains to sing, as people do for joy. With the sea and the world, all creation is called to rejoice before the LORD, who comes to judge the earth (verse 9). Isaiah 55:12 and Psalm 96:11-12 have a like picture.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: Let the rivers clap their hands, let the mountains sing together for joy
figure.means: the joy of all creation before the LORD, shown as if rivers and mountains could rejoice as people do

notes.evidence: Bullinger calls verses 7-8 a beautiful example of Personification, stressing the joy of the whole creation. Albert Barnes reads it as if the rivers were conscious and joined the praise. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): nature shares man's joy, high waves meeting like clapping hands. Henry and Benson: the floods rejoice as men do when they clap their hands, Henry adding, if they could.

cites.at: Prosopopoeia: human actions given to inanimate things, p. 865
cites.quote: are beautiful examples of Prosopopœia. It is a figure, of speech: but it emphasises the rejoicing of the whole creation of God, when Christ shall return to remove its curse, and cause its groanings to cease.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Let them join in the universal praise. As if conscious of their beauty, their grandeur, their usefulness; as if sensible that all this was conferred by God; as if rejoicing in the goodness of God manifested to them, and through them, let them unite in the universal praise.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In the bringing in of nature to participate in the joy of mankind, the clapping rivers (נהרות) are original to this Psalm: the rivers cast up high waves, which flow into one another like clapping hands
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Let the floods express their joy, as men do when they clap their hands; and let the hills, that trembled for fear before God when he came down to give the law at Mount Sinai, dance for joy before him when his gospel is preached … even the sea, and the floods, and the hills, would rejoice if they could.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He bids the sea roar, as men in triumph make a loud and vehement noise, and the floods to clap their hands, as men do in token of delight and approbation, while the hills, in like manner, resound their joy.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Lightning and clouds frame hail and snow
notes.about: The first four things named, which come down from the sky or rise toward it, can be read in a crossing order: the first answers the last, and the middle two answer each other. So lightning goes with clouds, and hail with snow.

lines.words: lightning
and hail,
snow
and clouds,

original.note: In Hebrew the first and last of the four are fire and smoke, which the BSB gives as lightning and clouds; the middle two are hail and snow.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the four, which come down from heaven or rise toward it, are arranged after the model of a chiasmus, a crosswise order, so that fire and smoke answer each other, and hail and snow.
notes.limit: Other writers take the four as two pairs in the order they are named, lightning with hail and snow with clouds, or group the clouds with the hail and snow as water in the sky. The crossing is one writer's reading.

cites.quote: Then to four phenomena of nature, coming down from heaven and ascending heavenwards, which are so arranged in Psa 148:8, after the model of the chiasmus (crosswise position), that fire and smoke ... hail and snow stand in reciprocal relation
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Walk, stand, sit: three steps further into sin
notes.about: The verse climbs in three steps: the blessed man does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, stand in the path of sinners, or sit among mockers. Each step goes further, from taking their advice to keeping their way to settling among scoffers, and many see the men grow worse at each step too.

lines.words: who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked,
or set foot on the path of sinners,
or sit in the seat of mockers.

original.note: In Hebrew the three verbs are walk, stand and sit; the BSB gives the second as “set foot.”

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anabasis: evil counsel is taken, then carried out, then settled in as on a seat. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) finds a climax in the three names for the wicked; Barnes a double climax in nouns and verbs, Clarke in the three characters and in walk, stand and sit. Calvin puts the seat at the top of the climax; Henry traces the steps to the height of impiety.
notes.limit: All the writers see the verse climb, but they place the climb differently: in the three names for the wicked, in walking, standing and sitting, or in counsel, path and seat. One doubts that the names rise, except for the mockers.

cites.quote: Here is a triple Anabasis depending on Parallelism … Again, the first continue in that mind, taking evil counsel. The second carry it out, as the principle of their walk. The third settle down in their evil, as on a seat.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The three appellations form a climax: impii corde, peccatores opere, illusores ore … Therefore: Blessed is he who does not walk in the state of mind which the ungodly cherish, much less that he should associate with the vicious life of sinners, or even delight in the company of those who scoff at religion.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We have here, then, a beautiful double gradation or climax, in the nouns and verbs of this verse, indicating successive stages of character. There is, first, casual walking with the wicked, or accidentally falling into their company; there is then a more deliberate inclination for their society
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: There is a double Climax in this verse, which it will be proper to note: - There are here three characters, each exceeding the other in sinfulness. … The second climax is found in the words, 1. Walk 2. Stand 3. Sit Which mark three different degrees of evil in the conduct of those persons.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The prophet, therefore, begins with counsel … Then he speaks of the way … And he places at the top of the climax the seat … In the same way, also, ought the three phrases, to walk, to stand, and to sit, to be understood. … Whether there is the same gradation in the Hebrew words … I leave to the judgment of others. To me it does not appear that there is, unless perhaps in the last word.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: They are here described by three characters, ungodly, sinners, and scornful. See by what steps men arrive at the height of impiety. … Omissions make way for commissions, and by these the heart is so hardened that at length they come to be scorners
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Ascribe to the LORD”, three times over
notes.about: Three lines in a row begin “Ascribe to the LORD”. The call comes again and again, pressing those addressed to give the LORD the glory due His name, as though they must be urged to it.

lines.words: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings,
ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.
Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name;

notes.evidence: Henry points out how often the call is repeated, once, again and a third time, and takes it to mean that the mighty are slow to this duty and hard to persuade. Calvin says the repetition shows that they must be strongly urged before they will give God His due.
notes.limit: The two writers who read the repetition as urging take those addressed as earthly rulers, slow to honor God; others take them as heavenly beings, as the BSB does.

cites.quote: How often this call is repeated; Give unto the Lord, and again, and a third time, Give unto the Lord. This intimates that the mighty men are backward to this duty and are with difficulty persuaded to it
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The repetition, also, shows that they must be vehemently urged ere a proper acknowledgement be extorted from them.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Glory and strength”: praise for what is His
notes.about: The heavenly beings are called to ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. He has both already, so the words stand for praising Him for His glory and strength, not for giving Him something He lacks.

figure.name: Metonymy
figure.means: the praise of His glory and strength, which are His already

original.note: In Hebrew the verb is havu, “give”; the BSB renders it “ascribe”.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metonymy: glory and strength cannot be given to God, so they are put for the praise given Him for them. Henry reads it as acknowledging His glory and strength and praising Him. Barnes: not granting God what He lacks, since He always has it, but owning Him as glorious and mighty. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) reads it as rendering back His glory and might in praise.
notes.limit: Some add a second sense: those called should also yield to Him whatever glory or strength He has given them.

cites.quote: How can we give these to God? We can praise Him for these, but we cannot give them. They are thus put, by Metonymy, for the praise given to Him for his glory and strength.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: nor as if we had any thing to give him that is not his own already (Who hath first given to him?), but the recognition of his glory, and of his dominion over us, he is pleased to interpret as a gift to him … Give unto the Lord glory and strength; acknowledge his glory and strength, and give praise to him as a God of infinite majesty and irresistible power
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Ascribe unto Yahweh; or, recognize Him as entitled to what is here ascribed to Him. The word cannot be understood, as it is commonly with us, to denote the imparting to another, or granting to another what he does not now possess - for God is always in possession of what is here ascribed to Him. … Glory and strength - Majesty and might. Acknowledge Him as the God of glory; as endowed with power.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: to render back to Him cheerfully and joyously in a laudatory recognition, as it were by an echo, His glory and might, which are revealed and to be revealed in the created world
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Seven lines open with “The voice of the LORD”
notes.about: Seven times a line begins with the same words, “The voice of the LORD.” They name the thunder and roar of a great storm, heard as God’s own voice, and their return line after line is the heart of the psalm.

lines.words: The voice of the LORD is over the waters;
The voice of the LORD is powerful;
the voice of the LORD is majestic.
The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars;
The voice of the LORD strikes with flames of fire.
The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness;
The voice of the LORD twists the oaks and strips the forests bare.

original.note: In Hebrew the phrase is two words, qol YHWH. Qol, voice, is used of any deep, rumbling sound, such as thunder.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists these verses, where the voice of the LORD begins seven clauses in a row. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the chief matter with the poet is the sevenfold voice of the LORD, the deep rumbling sound by which God makes Himself heard. Barnes notes that the phrase is seven times repeated in the psalm and refers to thunder, in which it seems as if God spoke.
notes.limit: The voice is chiefly the thunder of the storm; it can also take in the roar of the tempest and the quaking of the earth.

cites.quote: Where seven times, we have the words, “ The voice of the Lord,” commencing seven successive clauses.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The chief matter with the poet, however, is the sevenfold קול ה. ... The dull sounding קול serves not merely to denote the thunder of the storm, but even the thunder of the earthquake, the roar of the tempest, and in general, every low, dull, rumbling sound, by which God makes Himself audible to the world
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: There can be no doubt that the expression here, which is seven times repeated in the psalm, "the voice of Jehovah," refers to thunder; and no one can fail to see the appropriateness of the expression. In heavy thunder it seems as if God spake.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The LORD’s voice, His thunder, over the waters
notes.about: The three lines say one thing three ways. The voice of the LORD over the waters is His thunder, as the second line says: the God of glory thunders. The third line says it again: the LORD is heard over many waters.

lines.words: The voice of the LORD is over the waters;
the God of glory thunders;
the LORD is heard over many waters.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the poet himself explains the voice of the LORD as the thunder of the God of glory, rolling over the waters of the storm clouds. Henry explains the thunder of the God of glory as the noise of His voice, upon the waters and the many waters, over the ocean and among the clouds.
notes.limit: Writers differ on the waters: the waters gathered in the storm clouds, the sea, or both.

cites.quote: The rumbling ... of Jahve is, as the poet himself explains in Psa 29:3, the thunder produced on high by the אל הכּבוד ... which rolls over the sea of waters floating above the earth in the sky.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It is the God of glory that thunders (thunders is the noise of his voice ... ) ... To speak it the voice of the God of glory, it is here said to be upon the water, upon many waters ... it reaches over the vast ocean, the waters under the firmament; it rattles among the thick clouds, the waters above the firmament.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The cedars, then the cedars of Lebanon
notes.about: The first line speaks in general: the voice of the LORD breaks the cedars. The second takes it up and goes further, naming the cedars of Lebanon, the stateliest of all, so the storm is seen striking there.

lines.words: The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars;
the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the first line describes the storm in a general form and the second what is now taking place, the lightning riving the cedars of Lebanon, and he files this verse with verse 8 under the same kind of parallel. Henry reads the second line as going further: the thunder broke the cedars, even those of Lebanon, the strongest and stateliest.

cites.quote: Psa 29:5 describes this in a general form, and Psa 29:5 expresses by the fut. consec., as it were inferentially, that which is at present taking place: amidst the rolling of the thunder the descending lightning flashes rive the cedars of Lebanon ... as we are told in Psa 29:8 (cf. Psa 29:5, according to the schema of "parallelism by reservation")
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The voice of the Lord, in the thunder, often broke the cedars, even those of Lebanon, the strongest, the stateliest.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The wilderness, then the Wilderness of Kadesh
notes.about: The first line says the voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness. The second repeats it and names which wilderness, the Wilderness of Kadesh, far to the south.

lines.words: The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness;
the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the storm sweeps south into the desert, and the second line tells which: the wilderness of Kadesh, held back to be named there, as in verse 5. Barnes says that, as with Lebanon and Sirion, the psalmist names a particular place, Kadesh, to show the power of the tempest.
notes.limit: Writers differ on what is shaken: the desert, its sand whirled up by the storm, or the forests in it.

cites.quote: From the northern mountains the storm sweeps on towards the south of Palestine into the Arabian desert, viz., as we are told in Psa 29:8 (cf. Psa 29:5, according to the schema of "parallelism by reservation"), the wilderness region of Kadesh (Kadesh Barnea)
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As in referring Psa 29:5-6 to the effect of the storm on lofty trees, the psalmist had given poetic beauty to the description by "specifying" Lebanon and Sirion, so he here refers, for the same purpose, to a particular forest as illustrating the power of the tempest - to wit, the forest or wilderness of "Kadesh."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A refrain of trust: “The LORD of Hosts is with us”
notes.about: The same two lines come at verse 7 and again at verse 11, where the psalm ends: once after the nations rage, and once after God's call to be still. Each time His people answer with one confession: the LORD of Hosts is with them, and the God of Jacob is their fortress.

lines.words: The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.
The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.

original.note: In Hebrew the lines have no word for is, so they can speak of what God has been, is and will be to His people.

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls the words of verses 7 and 11 the burden, or refrain, of the song, and says the Hebrew takes in what God has been, is and will be. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says that after God's warning to the nations the church boasts yet once more that the LORD of Hosts is its God and stronghold. E. W. Bullinger lists the two verses as one phrase that comes twice.

cites.quote: It is the burden of the song, "The Lord of hosts is with us; he is on our side, he takes our part, is present with us and president over us; the God of Jacob is our refuge, to whom we may flee, and in whom we may confide and be sure of safety." ... The Lord of hosts, the God of Jacob, has been, is, and will be with us—has been, is and will be our refuge: the original includes all
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: With this admonition, which is both warning and threatening at the same time, the nations are dismissed; but the church yet once more boasts that Jahve Tsebaoth is its God and its stronghold.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Here, the phrase occurs twice, “The Lord of hosts is with us: the God of Jacob is our refuge.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: A line taken up again and carried to its end
notes.about: The second line takes up the words of the first, “surely Your enemies,” and carries them on to their end: they “will perish.” Saying the words again stresses how sure the end of God's enemies is.

lines.words: For surely Your enemies, O LORD,
surely Your enemies will perish;

original.note: In Hebrew the word the BSB gives as “surely” is hinneh, “behold,” said in both lines; it points to the enemies' end.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the repeat an emotional anadiplosis that breathes zeal for God's cause, the word behold pointing as with a finger to the enemies' inevitable end. Poole says the repeated words show their destruction as present and certain. Barnes calls the repeated lo emphatic, as of an event sure to occur.
notes.limit: Only one of the cited writers gives the repeat a name; the others speak of the repeated words and the certainty they give.

cites.quote: for lo Thine enemies, Jahve - for lo Thine enemies.... הנּה points as it were with the finger to the inevitable end; and the emotional anadiplosis breathes forth a zealous love for the cause of God as if it were his own.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He represents their destruction as present, and as certain, which the repetition of the words implies.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/psalms/92.htm

cites.quote: The repetition of the word "lo" here - "behold!" - is emphatic. The attention of the psalmist was fixed on this as an event which would be sure to occur.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The floods rise, then roar, then pound
notes.about: Each line takes up the one before and goes further: the floodwaters have risen, the rivers have raised their voice, the seas lift up their pounding waves. The noise can be read as growing into real danger, and the last line as telling of it still going on.

lines.words: The floodwaters have risen, O LORD;
the rivers have raised their voice;
the seas lift up their pounding waves.

original.note: In Hebrew all three lines use the same verb, “lift up”, and the same word, “rivers”; the BSB varies both, saying risen, raised and lift up, and floodwaters, rivers and seas.

notes.evidence: Henry reads the lines as rising: the floods lift up their voice, which speaks terror, and more than that their waves, which speaks real danger. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) renders the rivers as having lifted up, lifted up their murmur, and lifting up their roaring: a thought unfolded in what is called parallelism with reservation, the last verb telling of what is still taking place.
notes.limit: The note does not say what the floods stand for: some take them as the nations raging against God and His people, while others allow that the sea itself in a storm may be meant.

cites.quote: The floods have lifted up, O Lord! (to God himself the remonstrance is made) the floods have lifted up their voice, which speaks terror; nay, they have lifted up their waves, which speaks real danger.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: These rivers, as the poet says whilst he raises a plaintive but comforted look upwards to Jahve, have lifted up, have lifted up their murmur, the rivers lift up their roaring. The thought is unfolded in a so-called "parallelism with reservation." The perfects affirm what has taken place, the future that which even now as yet is taking place.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A question that says no one can praise Him enough
notes.about: The psalm asks who can tell all the mighty acts of the LORD or give Him all the praise He is due. The answer it expects is no one: His deeds are greater than any words. Some add that this is a reason to praise Him all the more, as best we can.

figure.name: Erotesis
figure.words: Who can describe the mighty acts of the LORD or fully proclaim His praise?
figure.means: no one can tell all His mighty deeds or praise Him as fully as He deserves

original.note: In Hebrew “proclaim” is a form of shama, to hear: to make His praise heard. “Mighty acts” is gevurot, the deeds that show His power.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Erotesis and gives the answer: no one can. Barnes says human language falls far short of His praises; Henry, that His acts are too many to number, too mysterious to describe. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls what God reveals inexhaustible, as in Psalm 40:5. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says His praise passes our speech; he and Henry say it urges us on.

cites.quote: “Who can utter the mighty acts of the Lord? who can show forth all his praise?” (Psa 106:2 ). The answer is that no one can.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: In other words, human language must fall immeasurably short of adequately expressing the praises of Yahweh, or conveying the fullness of what he has done. ... Hebrew, "Cause to be heard." That is, Language cannot be found which would cause "it to be heard" in a suitable manner.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Who can utter these? Who is worthy to do it? Who is able to do it? They are so many that they cannot be numbered, so mysterious that they cannot be described; when we have said the most we can of the mighty acts of the Lord, the one half is not told ... This will not excuse us in not doing what we can, but should quicken us to do all we can.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The fulness of this revelation, says Psa 106:2 (like Psa 40:6 ), is inexhaustible. גּבוּרות are the manifestations of His all-conquering power ... The proclaiming of these on the part of man can never be an exhaustive echo of them.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: His acts exceed our comprehension, as His praise our powers of expression ( Rom 11:33 ). Their unutterable greatness is not to keep us back, but to urge us the more to try to praise Him as best we can
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The psalmist asks the sea why it fled
notes.about: The psalmist turns to the sea and the Jordan, and then to the mountains and hills, and asks them, as if they could answer, why they fled and skipped. Verse 7 gives the answer: the presence of the Lord, before whom the earth is told to tremble.

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.words: Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back
figure.means: the sea and the Jordan, asked as if they could explain why they gave way before God's people

original.note: In Hebrew the question is abrupt, opening with mah lekha, literally what to you, O sea.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists verses 5 to 7 under Apostrophe to inanimate things. Barnes gives the Hebrew literally and says the psalmist speaks as if these lifeless things had been struck with terror and could be asked to explain themselves. Clarke calls the abrupt address a fine personification, then answered by the psalmist. Henry says the psalmist asks the sea in a poetical strain and gives it an answer.

cites.quote: “What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back? Ye mountains that ye skipped like rams? and ye little hills, like lambs? Tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord (Adon), at the presence of the God (Eloah) of Jacob.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: literally, "What to thee, O sea," etc. ... Instead of stating the cause or reason why they were thus thrown into dismay, the psalmist uses the language of surprise, as if these inanimate objects had been smitten with sudden terror, and as if it were proper to ask an explanation from themselves in regard to conduct that seemed so strange.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The original is very abrupt; and the prosopopoeia, or personification very fine and expressive ... After these very sublime interrogations, God appears; and the psalmist proceeds as if answering his own questions
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: To illustrate this the psalmist asks, in a poetical strain ... What ailed thee, O thou sea! that thou fleddest? And furnishes the sea with an answer ... The psalmist asks the mountains and hills what ailed them to skip thus; and he answers for them, as for the seas, it was at the presence of the Lord
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Will not slumber” rises to “nor sleep”
notes.about: Verse 4 takes up the words of verse 3 and goes a step higher: “your Protector will not slumber” becomes “the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.” The One who keeps each believer is the ever-wakeful Keeper of all His people.

lines.words: your Protector will not slumber.
Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the psalmist confirms that the Keeper will not slumber by heightening the words in verse 4, in keeping with the psalm's step-like movement. Barnes says verse 4 passes from the psalmist's own case to a general truth: the people of God are always safe, for their great Guardian never slumbers.

cites.quote: thy Keeper will surely not slumber; and then confirms the assertion that this shall not come to pass by heightening the expression in accordance with the step-like character of the Psalm: Behold the Keeper of Israel slumbereth not and sleepeth not
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The psalmist here passes from his own particular case to a general truth - a truth to him full of consolation. It is, that the people of God must always be safe; that their great Guardian never slumbers
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “His loving devotion endures forever,” 26 times
notes.about: Every verse ends with the same line. At the temple’s dedication the people gave thanks in the same words (2 Chronicles 7:3).

notes.short: “O my soul”: the psalmist calls on himself
notes.about: Having called on all to praise the LORD, the psalmist turns and speaks to his own soul, that is, to himself. He stirs up his own heart first, before he leads others, and the next verse gives his answer: “I will praise the LORD all my life.”

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.means: the psalmist himself, his inner self, whom he calls to praise

original.note: In Hebrew the word is nephesh, “soul”, which here is put for the psalmist himself.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Apostrophe to one's own self, the soul being put for the self. Calvin says the psalmist, having called on all to praise, addresses himself, his soul, to name his inward self with more emphasis, and stirs his own zeal before leading others. Henry says David stirred himself up to the work with these words.

cites.at: Apostrophe to one’s own self, p. 903
cites.quote: This is done by the common Hebrew idiom, by which one’s “soul” is put (by Synecdoche) for one’s self. ... So Psa 104:1; Psa 146:1, etc.

notes.short: The psalm begins and ends with “Hallelujah!”
notes.about: The psalm opens and closes with the same word, “Hallelujah!”, a call to all to praise the LORD. Between the two stand the warning against trust in princes and the praise of the God who helps the needy and reigns forever. The last five psalms all begin and end this way.

lines.words: Hallelujah!
Hallelujah!

original.note: In Hebrew it is hallelu-yah, “praise the LORD”, spoken to many; the same two words open and close the psalm.

notes.evidence: Calvin says the five last psalms close with the same word with which they begin. Barnes, at verse 10, says the psalm closes as it commences, with Hallelujah, a call on all to praise. Benson says it begins and ends with Hallelujah, as do all the rest to the end of the book.

cites.quote: The five last Psalms close with the same word with which they begin.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Praise ye the Lord - Hallelu-jah. The psalm closes as it commences. It is a call on all persons to unite in the praise of Yahweh.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It begins and ends with Hallelujah, or, Praise ye the Lord, as do all the rest to the end of the book, which have therefore been styled, The hallelujahs.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Five lines in a row begin with “the LORD”
notes.about: Five short lines in a row begin with the same words, “the LORD”: He frees prisoners, opens blind eyes, lifts the weighed down, loves the righteous and protects foreigners. The repeated name can be read as stressing that it is the LORD's own almighty power at work for the oppressed.

lines.words: The LORD sets the prisoners free,
the LORD opens the eyes of the blind,
the LORD lifts those who are weighed down,
the LORD loves the righteous.
The LORD protects foreigners;

original.note: In Hebrew each of these lines is only three words long, and each begins with the name of the LORD, YHWH.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the five lines beginning with the LORD's name belong together, each of three words. Henry says the name is repeated five times in five lines, to show that the LORD's almighty power is engaged for the relief of the oppressed.

cites.quote: The five lines beginning with Jahve belong together. Each consists of three words, which in the main is also the favourite measure of the lines in the Book of Job.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It ought not to pass without remark that the name of Jehovah is repeated here five times in five lines, to intimate that it is an almighty power (that of Jehovah) that is engaged and exerted for the relief of the oppressed
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The LORD helps the needy but frustrates the wicked
notes.about: After line on line of the LORD's help for the needy, one line answers with the opposite: He frustrates the ways of the wicked. Help fills many lines and judgment only one, which can be read as showing that He delights most to rule in love.

lines.words: He sustains the fatherless and the widow,
but the ways of the wicked He frustrates.

original.note: In Hebrew the verb is a picture of bending: the LORD bends the way of the wicked, so that it leads astray.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) sets the two against each other: while the LORD gives the sorrows of His saints a blessed end, He bends the way of the wicked into error, pointing to Psalm 1:6. This judging has only one line, he says, for the LORD rules in love and in wrath but delights most to rule in love.

cites.quote: Whilst Jahve, however, makes the manifold sorrows of His saints to have a blessed issue, He bends ... the way of the wicked, so that it leads into error and ends in the abyss (Psa 1:6). This judicial manifestation of Jahve has only one line devoted to it. For He rules in love and in wrath, but delights most of all to rule in love.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “The fatherless and the widow”: all the helpless
notes.about: The verse names the fatherless and the widow, but they stand for more than themselves: one kind of helpless people is put for every kind. The LORD who sustains them sustains all the afflicted.

figure.name: Synecdoche
figure.means: all kinds of afflicted and helpless people, of whom these are one kind

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Synecdoche of the Species, where widows and fatherless are put for all kinds of afflicted: one class stands for all similar kinds of helpless people.

cites.quote: Widows and Fatherless are put for all kinds of afflicted ... one kind or class is put for all similar kinds of helpless people. ... So also Psa 146:9.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Ten lines in a row begin “Praise”
notes.about: Line after line begins with the same call, praise, ten times over. The call is pressed again and again, which shows how great a duty praise is; the count of ten can also be read as a sign of fullness.

lines.words: Praise God in His sanctuary.
Praise Him in His mighty heavens.
Praise Him for His mighty acts;
praise Him for His excellent greatness.
Praise Him with the sound of the horn;
praise Him with the harp and lyre.
Praise Him with tambourine and dancing;
praise Him with strings and flute.
Praise Him with clashing cymbals;
praise Him with resounding cymbals.

original.note: In Hebrew each of the ten calls is a form of halal, praise, the verb inside Hallelujah.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the whole psalm with those where praise is repeated at the beginning of successive sentences. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) counts ten calls to praise set between the Hallelujahs, takes ten as the number of completeness, and goes through them one by one. Henry says the call is repeated so often because praise is a great and necessary duty, to which we are by nature cold.
notes.limit: That the ten calls stand for completeness is one reading; the repeated call itself is plain.

cites.quote: Psa 148:1-4. -“ Praise ” is seven times repeated at the beginning of successive sentences. So also in the whole of Psa 150:1-6
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: in the mind of the poet the tenfold halaluw encompassed by Hallelujah's is significative; for ten is the number of rounding off, completeness, exclusiveness, and of the extreme of exhaustibleness. ... The third and fourth hălalu give as the object of the praise that which is at the same time the ground of the praise
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We are here, with the greatest earnestness imaginable, excited to praise God ... And the repeated inculcating of the call thus intimates that it is a great and necessary duty, a duty which we should be much employed and much enlarged in, but which we are naturally backward to and cold in

notes.short: The psalm opens and closes with “Hallelujah!”
notes.about: The psalm begins and ends with the same word, Hallelujah, and the ten calls to praise God stand between the two.

lines.words: Hallelujah!
Hallelujah!

original.note: In Hebrew Hallelujah is halelu-Yah, praise the LORD; the ten calls between use the same verb, halal.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the ten calls to praise are encompassed by Hallelujahs, the word that opens and closes the psalm, and that the poet means the number to be significant.

cites.quote: in the mind of the poet the tenfold halaluw encompassed by Hallelujah's is significative; for ten is the number of rounding off, completeness

notes.short: His sanctuary is His mighty heavens
notes.about: The second line says the first again: the sanctuary where God is to be praised is His heaven, the mighty expanse above. Both lines lift the eyes to God enthroned on high.

lines.words: Praise God in His sanctuary.
Praise Him in His mighty heavens.

original.note: In Hebrew the heavens are the raqia, the expanse spread out above, called mighty for the power it shows.

notes.evidence: Calvin says the sanctuary here is heaven and the second clause explains the first, repeating the same thing with the expanse of heaven. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says both places in the verse are heavenly: the sanctuary is the heavenly temple, and the firmament is seen from its heavenly side.
notes.limit: Others take the sanctuary to be the temple on earth, so that the two lines call for praise on earth and in heaven.

cites.quote: By the sanctuary there is little doubt that heaven is here meant, as is often the case elsewhere. The second clause is exegetical, for the same thing is repeated. But for sanctuary we read רקיע, rekia, that is, the expanse of heaven, to which is added the epithet of power ... That the majesty of God may be duly reverenced, the Psalmist represents him as presiding on his throne in the heavens
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The local definitions in Psa 150:1 are related attributively to God, and designate that which is heavenly, belonging to the other world, as an object of praise. ... is in this passage the heavenly היכל; and ... is the firmament spread out by God's omnipotence ... according to the reverse or inner side, which is turned towards the celestial world
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A bed flooded with tears tells of deep grief
notes.about: David says, “all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears.” The words say more than is literally meant. They show in strong terms how many tears he shed and how deep his sorrow went, worn out as he was from groaning.

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.words: flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears
figure.means: how many tears he shed and how deep his sorrow went

original.note: In Hebrew the word for “drench” means to melt or flow down: he made his couch flow with tears.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse with other hyperbolical pictures of weeping. Barnes calls it hyperbolical language for the depth of David's sorrow, and says the verb rendered water (here drench) means to melt or flow down; and Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says a strong figure shows how much and how deeply he grieved.

cites.quote: This is an hyperbolical description of the intensity of their weeping and lamentation. Similar descriptions occur Psa 6:6; Psa 119:136.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: All the night make I my bed to swim - That is, he wept so much that his bed seemed to be immersed in tears. This is, of course, hyperbolical language, expressing in a strong and emphatic manner the depth of his sorrows. I water my couch with my tears - The word here rendered "water" means to melt, to flow down; then, in the Hiphil, to cause to flow, to dissolve.

cites.quote: By a strong figure the abundance as well as intensity of grief is depicted.
